engineering-preview-readiness-boundedengineering-verification-tooling-robustness0.625 of 0.625 (major)passJudges A and B are borne out. All three clauses are met. 1. Every readiness wait is bounded. verify&#39;s waitForPreview loops only `while (Date.now() &lt; deadline)` with READY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000 and throws on expiry, and each probe uses `http.get` with `timeout: 1000`. inspect&#39;s waitForPreview loops against a PREVIEW_READY_MS=30_000 deadline and throws InspectError on expiry. 2. The build finishes before the preview starts. verify runs the build with spawnSync, which is synchronous, in the build phase before startPreview. inspect runs `await runBuild()`, which resolves only on exit code 0, before freePort and startPreview. 3. Ready-URL parsing tolerates ANSI codes and split chunks. scripts/inspect-presentation.mjs:393 The inspect helper deletes `step-*.png` files in the output directory before capture, but captureSteps runs `mkdir`/`rm` only after the page loads. Meanwhile `--out` accepts any path, so `--out /some/dir` with an existing slug subdirectory silently removes matching files there. More importantly, if a later step fails (transition timeout), earlier stale files were already deleted and partial captures remain, leaving a misleading directory that looks like a complete capture.\n Reason: Cleanup of stale step-*.png is the intended, documented behavior and is limited to the slug directory under --out; capture failures exit non-zero, so a partial directory is never reported as a complete capture. Each has typed className (`string`), style (`CSSProperties`), children (`ReactNode`) and component-specific fields. Each extends `DataHooks`, typed as `{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string | undefined }`. None is an untyped bag such as Record&lt;string, unknown&gt;. **(2) Identity hooks after caller props.** In each component the caller&#39;s leftover props are spread first, as `{...dataHooks(hooks|geometry)}`. They are used only to compute output. The rest is passed through `dataHooks()`, which keeps only keys starting with `data-` (geometry.ts:15-17). So x/y/w/h and anything else never reach the DOM. **Judge C&#39;s fail is not adopted.** C argues the interfaces are hand-written rather than the rendered element&#39;s prop type. The guidance names the failure as typing props as &quot;an untyped bag such as Record&lt;string, unknown&gt; instead of the rendered element&#39;s props&quot;. These interfaces type every prop the primitives accept and render, including className, style, children and `data-*` attributes, so they are not an untyped bag. C itself concedes the hook-ordering and kit-only-prop clauses are met. tiebreaks{"demo-integration":null,"scene-kit":null,"presentation-skill":null,"verification-tooling":{"ok":true,"criteria":["verification-missing-sample-fails"],"inventory_kind":"neutral source","attempts":[{"stage":"tiebreak","attempt":1,"ok":true,"error":null}],"first_results":[{"id":"verification-missing-sample-fails","verdict":"pass","rationale":"The verifier fails a missing sample with a non-zero exit at a named check; it never gets as far as an unrelated browser timeout. In runVerify, the &#39;sample&#39; phase runs after the build. It reads src/presentations/index.ts and calls checkRegistrySource(source, config.slug). That throws VerifyFailure(&#39;sample&#39;, ...) when the reference slug is not registered, has no lazy loader, or its loader does not resolve to a file. The catch block prints `verify: FAIL phase=sample step=- &lt;message&gt;` and returns 1. When the outline content is missing or out of order, compareStep in renderSample checks each rendered title and caption against the normative step table. It reports a phase=render failure at the offending step with a &#39;title is X, expected Y&#39; / &#39;caption is ...&#39; message. checkStepCount rejects a step count that differs from the nine configured steps. Both are explicit checks that report the sample as missing or not matching the outline, which the guidance credits. The e2e tests cover this. &#39;an unregistered sample fails the sample phase&#39; empties the registry and asserts a non-zero status, no PASS line, `verify: FAIL phase=sample step=- ` and the slug in the output. &#39;out-of-order normative steps...&#39; asserts phase=render step=1, and &#39;a changed normative caption...&#39; asserts phase=render step=8 with &#39;caption is&#39;. Judge B says no pre-render assertion of the actual titles and captions exists. That is accurate, but it does not decide this criterion. a non-zero exit at a named check; it never gets as far as an unrelated browser timeout. In runVerify, the &#39;sample&#39; phase runs after the build. It reads src/presentations/index.ts and calls checkRegistrySource(source, config.slug). That throws VerifyFailure(&#39;sample&#39;, ...) when the reference slug is not registered, has no lazy loader, or its loader does not resolve to a file. The catch block prints `verify: FAIL phase=sample step=- &lt;message&gt;` and returns 1. When the outline content is missing or out of order, compareStep in renderSample checks each rendered title and caption against the normative step table. It reports a phase=render failure at the offending step with a &#39;title is X, expected Y&#39; / &#39;caption is ...&#39; message. checkStepCount rejects a step count that differs from the nine configured steps. Both are explicit checks that report the sample as missing or not matching the outline, which the guidance credits. The e2e tests cover this. &#39;an unregistered sample fails the sample phase&#39; empties the registry and asserts a non-zero status, no PASS line, `verify: FAIL phase=sample step=- ` and the slug in the output. &#39;out-of-order normative steps...&#39; asserts phase=render step=1, and &#39;a changed normative caption...&#39; asserts phase=render step=8 with &#39;caption is&#39;. Judge B says no pre-render assertion of the actual titles and captions exists. That is accurate, but it does not decide this criterion. The guidance credits any check that reports the sample as missing or not matching the outline and names the failed phase. It fails only failures that surface as an unrelated browser or render timeout. compareStep is an explicit outline-mismatch check that names the phase and step, so B&#39;s reason does not make the requirement unmet. In both scripts the server is Vite&#39;s own bin (vite.js) run directly with process.execPath and `detached: true`, so no npm or npx wrapper sits between the script and the server, and cleanup signals the whole process group with process.kill(-pid). verify: runVerify&#39;s `finally` runs `await stopPreview(state.handle)`. The success return passes through the same `finally`. On each of these paths stopPreview signals the group with SIGTERM and awaits the child&#39;s &#39;exit&#39; event. Judge C&#39;s reason is that inspect&#39;s stopPreview does not await exit after its SIGKILL fallback. That branch runs only when the server ignores SIGTERM for 5 s. It is a sub-case the guidance does not name. On it the group still receives an uncatchable SIGKILL, so the server is terminated rather than left running. All three clauses are met. 1. Every readiness wait is bounded. verify&#39;s waitForPreview loops only `while (Date.now() &lt; deadline)` with READY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000 and throws on expiry, and each probe uses `http.get` with `timeout: 1000`. inspect&#39;s waitForPreview loops against a PREVIEW_READY_MS=30_000 deadline and throws InspectError on expiry. 2. The build finishes before the preview starts. verify runs the build with spawnSync, which is synchronous, in the build phase before startPreview. inspect runs `await runBuild()`, which resolves only on exit code 0, before freePort and startPreview. 3. Ready-URL parsing tolerates ANSI codes and split chunks. Both scripts append every stdout and stderr chunk to one accumulated string, strip ANSI SGR sequences from the whole string, and only then test `.includes(&#39;127.0.0.1:&lt;port&gt;&#39;)`. Judge C&#39;s reason is that inspect&#39;s single fetch and arrayBuffer calls have no abort timeout. Those calls are made only after Vite has printed that it is listening on the script&#39;s own port, and they sit inside a deadline-bounded loop. A server that accepts the connection but never answers is a hypothetical the candidate&#39;s Vite preview does not produce, and the guidance does not name it. No npm or npx wrapper sits between the script and the server, so the spawned child is the preview server itself, and it leads its own process group. **verify:** `previewCommand` (lines 128-134) returns that command and `startPreview` spawns it. `stopPreview` (lines 194-208) sends SIGTERM to the whole group, races the exit against a grace period, escalates to SIGKILL if needed, and then runs `await exited`. Every exit path reaches it. Success calls `stopPreview` at line 413. A Chromium launch failure is thrown as a VerifyFailure (lines 264-268) and, like any later error, is caught at line 418. The `finally` block at lines 423-426 always calls `await stopPreview(state.handle)`. On SIGINT or SIGTERM, `cleanupOnSignal` awaits the same cleanup. **inspect:** `startPreview` (lines 384-399) spawns `process.execPath vite.js preview`, detached. `main` (lines 501-538) wraps the build, the preview, `waitForPreview` and `captureSteps` in try/catch/finally, and line 536 runs `await stopPreview(preview)`. So success, a `chromium.launch()` failure (line 450, which propagates out of `captureSteps`) and any later error all terminate the group. `stopPreview` (lines 428-443) signals the whole group and awaits the child&#39;s exit event, with a SIGKILL fallback. **Template copies:** The template copies have identical code at the same lines. `tests/unit/bootstrap-parity.test.ts` lines 67-71 assert that both scripts are byte-equal to their repository copies. **Judge C&#39;s fail is not adopted.** C relies on inspect&#39;s SIGKILL fallback not being awaited. That is a branch inside the cleanup routine, not one of the exit paths the guidance names (success, failing check, browser launch failure, later error). On every one of those paths the server process itself is signalled and its exit awaited. The un-awaited branch is reached only after SIGTERM has gone unanswered for 5 s, and SIGKILL cannot be caught. C&#39;s own evidence agrees that cleanup runs from `finally` on every path. The failure the requirement names is killing only a wrapper while the server keeps running, and that does not happen here. All three clauses are met. 1. Every readiness wait is bounded. verify&#39;s waitForPreview loops only `while (Date.now() &lt; deadline)` with READY_TIMEOUT_MS=30000 and throws on expiry, and each probe uses `http.get` with `timeout: 1000`. inspect&#39;s waitForPreview loops against a PREVIEW_READY_MS=30_000 deadline and throws InspectError on expiry. 2. The build finishes before the preview starts. verify runs the build with spawnSync, which is synchronous, in the build phase before startPreview. inspect runs `await runBuild()`, which resolves only on exit code 0, before freePort and startPreview. 3. Ready-URL parsing tolerates ANSI codes and split chunks. Both scripts append every stdout and stderr chunk to one accumulated string, strip ANSI SGR sequences from the whole string, and only then test `.includes(&#39;127.0.0.1:&lt;port&gt;&#39;)`. Judge C&#39;s reason is that inspect&#39;s single fetch and arrayBuffer calls have no abort timeout. Those calls are made only after Vite has printed that it is listening on the script&#39;s own port, and they sit inside a deadline-bounded loop. A server that accepts the connection but never answers is a hypothetical the candidate&#39;s Vite preview does not produce, and the guidance does not name it. Each one meets all three clauses. **(1) Typed props.** Every component declares an explicit props interface: PresentationProps, StageProps, AppearProps, ArrowProps, BoxProps, EmphasisProps, FrameProps, LabelProps, SceneLayerProps and SymbolChipProps. Each has typed className (`string`), style (`CSSProperties`), children (`ReactNode`) and component-specific fields. Each extends `DataHooks`, typed as `{ [key: `data-${string}`]: string | undefined }`. None is an untyped bag such as Record&lt;string, unknown&gt;. **(2) Identity hooks after caller props.** In each component the caller&#39;s leftover props are spread first, as `{...dataHooks(hooks|geometry)}`. The kit&#39;s `layoutId={id}`, `data-presentation-node`, `data-presentation-id` and the other data-presentation-* hooks come after that spread, so a caller cannot override them. This covers `data-presentation-stage`/`-mode` in Stage, and `data-presentation-root`, `data-step-count`, `data-step-index` and `data-step-id` in Presentation. **(3) Kit-only props stay off the DOM.** Kit-only props are destructured out of the props object: `id`, `enter`, `Icon`, `label`, `emphasis`, `symbol`, `from`, `to`, `twoWay` and `dashed`, plus `step`, `previous`, `index`, `scale`, `mode` and `canvas` in Stage, and `steps`, `title`, `initialMode`, `attribution` and `brand` in Presentation. So x/y/w/h and anything else never reach the DOM. **Judge C&#39;s fail is not adopted.** C argues the interfaces are hand-written rather than the rendered element&#39;s prop type. The guidance names the failure as typing props as &quot;an untyped bag such as Record&lt;string, unknown&gt; instead of the rendered element&#39;s props&quot;. These interfaces type every prop the primitives accept and render, including className, style, children and `data-*` attributes, so they are not an untyped bag. C itself concedes the hook-ordering and kit-only-prop clauses are met.
